cases.scenario: Sales says the MQLs are bad. Tier A converts at 12.4% versus tier D at 2.1%, but only 41% of tier A leads are ever touched against 38% of tier C.
pass_if: Leads with the diagnosis that the score works and the list is not being worked
Gives both the separation figures and the coverage figures with their samples
States that near-identical touch rates across tiers means the score has not been tested rather than disproven
Notes that tier A converts better despite equal effort, which strengthens the lift's credibility
Recommends routing and SLA changes rather than rebuilding the model
Checks whether variation by rep exceeds variation by tier
fail_if: Concludes the score is broken from the sales complaint
Reports the lift without the action-coverage analysis

cases.scenario: Four tiers. B converts at 8.1% (CI 6.9-9.3) and C at 6.9% (CI 5.8-8.0), on samples of about 2,000 each.
pass_if: States that B and C do not differ significantly and that their intervals overlap
Says in plain terms that four tiers are doing the work of three
Recommends merging them and frames the merge as an improvement, not a retreat
Runs the omnibus test before the pairwise comparisons and corrects for multiple comparisons
Reports the effect size in operational terms, not only significance
fail_if: Runs six pairwise tests with no correction

cases.scenario: A score shows excellent retrospective lift. Median lead time between crossing the threshold and the outcome is minus 2 days, and 44% of conversions had their crossing on or after the outcome date.
pass_if: Identifies the score as lagging confirmation rather than a prioritisation tool
Gives the share-at-or-after figure as the diagnostic evidence
Explains why retrospective lift looks excellent for a lagging score
Identifies the actions with near-zero lead time as the cause and proposes removing them or splitting the score into early-intent and late-confirmation components
Does not report the retrospective lift as evidence the score is useful for prioritisation
fail_if: Reports the lift as proof the score works
Discards the score without identifying which actions cause the lag

cases.scenario: Tier A converts at 3.1x the base rate. Tier A leads are touched at 87% versus tier C at 34%. No holdout exists.
pass_if: Reports the 3.1x lift
States that tier A is worked far harder, so some of the lift is follow-up rather than lead quality
Attempts to bound it: conditions on comparable touch counts and reports the result
Searches for a natural experiment such as a capacity gap or vacation window
Names the randomised holdout as what would settle it, with a realistic size
Does not withhold the lift figure because it is confounded
fail_if: Reports the lift with no self-fulfilling-prophecy caveat
Withholds the lift because of the confound
Presents the conditioned comparison as if it were causal proof

cases.scenario: A year-over-year comparison of scoring performance is requested. The scoring rules changed in April.
pass_if: States that the comparison spans two score versions and that the score is a different quantity on each side
Offers the within-version comparison and the re-scored alternative, naming what each costs
Marks the change on any trendline that crosses it
Gives the numbers available within each version rather than refusing the whole request
fail_if: Produces the year-over-year comparison without disclosure
Treats the rules change as a data-quality issue to be cleaned

cases.scenario: A scoring evaluation cohort includes records scored in the last three weeks, with a 90-day outcome horizon.
pass_if: Excludes records whose outcome horizon has not elapsed and reports how many were excluded
States that including them enters them as negatives and depresses every tier rate
Requires cohorting by scoring date rather than outcome date
Requires the score snapshot from the time rather than the current recomputed score
fail_if: Uses the current score for historical records
